analysis.one_liner: Designates millions of acres of Northern Rockies federal land as wilderness and bans road building, logging, mining, and oil and gas drilling there.
analysis.headline: The bill to protect millions of acres of Northern Rockies wildland never received a hearing or vote in the Senate committee it was sent to.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would put millions of acres of federal land in Idaho, Montana, Oregon, Washington, and Wyoming into the National Wilderness Preservation System, add wild and scenic river designations, and connect the region's big ecosystems with wildlife corridors. It would ban road building, logging, mining, and oil and gas leasing on the designated roadless lands. It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, people who hunt, fish, hike, and recreate in the Northern Rockies would gain permanently protected backcountry, and communities downstream of the Columbia, Snake, and Missouri headwaters would benefit from protected watersheds. Taxpayers would stop subsidizing timber sales the bill's findings describe as below-cost, and the bill would fund restoration work that creates jobs in outdoor trades.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hunters, anglers, hikers, and local communities

how_it_helps.text: Permanently protects as wilderness millions of acres of national forest, national park, and Bureau of Land Management land across Idaho, Montana, Oregon, Washington, and Wyoming, including large additions to existing wildernesses and new wilderness in Yellowstone and Glacier national parks.
Connects the region's major ecosystems with designated biological corridors so wildlife such as grizzly bears, wolves, and lynx can move and interbreed as climate conditions shift.
Bans road construction, timber harvest, oil and gas leasing, and mining on covered roadless lands, protecting water quality in the headwaters of the Columbia, Snake, and Missouri river systems.
Creates wildland recovery areas where federal agencies must develop restoration plans, work the bill's findings say would create employment in outdoor trades and contracts for local businesses.
Lets the Interior and Agriculture Departments accept donated grazing permits, a voluntary mechanism that retires grazing on sensitive public lands while compensating permit holders.

analysis.who_pays: If passed, timber companies would lose areas now open to logging, mining companies would lose areas open to claims and exploration, and oil and gas companies could not lease designated roadless lands. Some rural communities in the region that depend on resource-extraction work would bear the adjustment costs, and some motorized-recreation users would lose access to designated areas.

drawbacks.text: Locking up land from timber harvest, mining, and energy development would eliminate some existing and potential extraction jobs and revenue in rural communities that depend on those industries, a trade-off the bill's own findings acknowledge by citing economic instability in resource-dependent towns.

The bill was written and sponsored entirely by senators from outside the five affected states, bypassing the local forest-planning processes and state input that usually shape land designations, which made political support in the region unlikely.
Wilderness designation bans motorized recreation and new development broadly, including ski-resort facilities, so some current users of these public lands would lose the access they have today.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are large and permanent: protected watersheds, wildlife corridors, and recreation access on millions of acres, plus an end to below-cost subsidized logging the bill's findings describe as a taxpayer loss. The costs are real but narrower: lost extraction jobs and revenue concentrated in a handful of rural counties, and lost motorized access for some users. The bill's biggest practical weakness was political, not substantive: it was a sweeping, all-at-once designation pushed by out-of-region senators with no local cosponsors, in a committee controlled by a senator from a coal state, so it never came close to a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 21, 2021 and read twice before being referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee.

It would have designated wilderness across Idaho, Montana, Oregon, Washington, and Wyoming, including roughly 2,030,000 acres of Yellowstone National Park and 925,000 acres of Glacier National Park, and dozens of new wilderness areas on national forest and Bureau of Land Management land.

It would have prohibited road construction, timber harvest, oil and gas leasing, mining, and other development that impairs the natural and roadless qualities of covered lands, and would have let the Interior and Agriculture Departments accept donations of grazing permits to retire them.

The bill had 11 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents, none of them from the five affected states; the listed sponsors were senators from Rhode Island, New Jersey, Connecticut, Illinois, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Ohio, and Hawaii.
The Energy and Natural Resources Committee took no action on the bill after referral, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 without the bill ever receiving a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Timber, mining, and oil and gas interests are better off, since they keep the current access to these lands that the bill would have taken away. The status quo also stands for recreationists and local communities, with no new protections but no new restrictions.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Timber, mining, and oil and gas interests

for.name: Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled a bloc of cosponsors for it.

against.name: Joe Manchin
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; the committee took no action on it after referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 cosponsors were Democrats or independents and no Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and it died without action in the Democratic-chaired Energy and Natural Resources Committee.

industries.note: The bill bans timber harvest on designated lands and its findings argue below-cost federal timber sales lose taxpayer money. Logging access to millions of acres would end.
Mining is expressly prohibited on covered roadless lands, closing new claims and exploration across the designated area.
The bill prohibits oil and gas leasing on designated roadless lands, removing those areas from future drilling and exploration.
The bill lets federal agencies accept donated grazing permits, giving ranchers a way to sell out permits for conservation, while locking in protection over grazing landscapes.
The bill would expand protected backcountry for hunting, fishing, and wilderness-based recreation, and fund restoration work that creates contracts for local businesses.
